summary:
Cosmic Symphony is a 2D pixel-art browser game for kids aged 7–12, built for the "Build a Junior Astronaut Mission Trainer" challenge. Each player becomes a Commander running their own Moon base. They walk Pip-7, a robot guide, around the base and go inside eight buildings, including a Greenhouse, Habitat and Storm Shelter. Each building has hands-on stations and mini-games. Kids grow plants, keep the crew warm through the 14-day lunar night, build radiation shields and supervise a rover's AI. Coins they earn pay for building upgrades, which unlock harder activities.

The game teaches the real trade-offs astronauts face. Every building uses power, every crew member needs air, and using more than you make browns out the base. Four story-driven Big Missions take players from the Moon to Mars.

The science comes from real NASA open data: live solar storms from DONKI, plant-biology studies from OSDR, and today's Earth–Mars radio delay calculated from JPL orbit data. Each activity has a short animated how-to-play video, and a Knowledge Card collection rewards learning.

This matters because space science can feel distant and abstract. Cosmic Symphony turns it into play, so children learn the trade-offs real explorers face before they've even learned the word "engineering".
details:
What does it do and how does it work?

Cosmic Symphony is a 2D pixel-art browser game for kids aged 7–12 that turns NASA science into play. Each player is a Commander running their own Moon base with Pip-7, a friendly robot guide. They walk Pip around the base, go inside buildings, try hands-on science stations, play short arcade games to earn coins, and spend those coins on upgrades that unlock harder activities.

The player's Moon base, with the coins, power meters and Pip's next task floating on top of the world.

The base has eight buildings, and each one is a themed room with stations that teach through doing:

  • Greenhouse: grow plants by balancing water, light and plant food.
  • Habitat: keep the crew warm through the 14-day lunar night.
  • Storm Shelter: build a radiation wall within a rocket's mass limit.
  • Rover Garage: design a rover and supervise its AI.Inside the Greenhouse, where every station teaches one science idea.A station activity, where kids change real variables and see the result.

    Behind everything is a real engineering trade-off. Every building uses power and only the Solar Array makes it, so using too much causes a brownout. Every crew member who breathes also needs life support.

There are seven arcade mini-games, including Storm Shield and Rover Dash, which simulates the radio delay to Mars. In Mission Control, players pick one of four story-driven Big Missions, from the Moon to Mars. Finishing a mission adds an instrument to the base's "Cosmic Symphony".

The Mission Board, where players choose one of four Big Missions.

A Big Mission in which a real solar storm from NASA's records heads toward the base.

The science uses real NASA open data:

  • NASA DONKI: live solar storms drive Storm Shield and the space-weather alerts.
  • NASA OSDR: plant-biology and radiation studies support the greenhouse and radiation lessons.
  • NASA JPL orbit data: today's real Earth–Mars radio delay is calculated in the browser.
  • NASA Image and Video Library: the real photos come from here, each credited.

If a live service is down, the game shows archived NASA records and labels them as archived.

What benefits does it have?

Kids learn by doing instead of reading. They don't read that plants need light: they set the lamp hours and watch the plant thrive or wilt. Wrong answers are never a dead end, because Pip explains why and the player tries again. Learning earns Knowledge Cards, 16 in total, and progress is saved to the player's account so they can continue on any device.The Collection, where kids keep the Knowledge Cards they earn by learning.

What is the intended impact?

Space science can feel far away to a 7-year-old. Cosmic Symphony turns it into something kids can touch, so they understand the trade-offs astronauts face before they've even learned the word "engineering". We hope teachers and parents use it as a playful first step into STEM, building curiosity about how astronauts survive and why NASA explores.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did we use?

  • Code: HTML5, CSS3 and plain JavaScript, with no frameworks and no build step. It runs in any modern browser on a laptop, tablet or phone.
  • Graphics: HTML5 Canvas 2D for the pixel-art engine and all scenes.
  • Sound: the Web Audio API synthesizes all music and sound effects live, with no audio files.
  • Accounts: Supabase Authentication for email or Google login, with each player's progress saved online.
  • Server: a small Node.js server that serves the game and relays NASA OSDR requests.
  • NASA data: DONKI, OSDR, JPL Solar System Dynamics and the NASA Image and Video Library.
  • Testing: Node's built-in test runner checks the science simulations, and scripted browser playtests run through every building, station and game.

How is the project creative?

  • Exploration is the menu. Kids walk a character around a living base and into rooms instead of clicking through screens.
  • Video guides. Every station and game has a short animated how-to-play clip, drawn live in the game's own pixel style. It plays the first time, can be skipped, and can be rewatched from an ⓘ button.
  • Made entirely in code. All art is pixel sprites drawn in code, and each area of the base has its own chiptune soundtrack generated in the browser.
  • Progress you can hear. Each completed Big Mission adds an instrument to the Cosmic Symphony.
    Unlock Crew to discover more characters.
